title: Keeping Agents on a Leash: An Eight-Domain Control Model for AI Agents with Delegated Authority
abstract: Design / position paper. An agent with delegated authority is an attack surface with credentials. The research answer is defenses evaluated on benchmarks, and those benchmarks are sobering: indirect prompt injection still succeeds between 10.7% and 29.6% against frontier models in production-like settings (LivePI), and of ten recent defenses on open-ended tasks almost all are either insufficiently secure or significantly over-defensive (AgentDyn). Operators must nevertheless ship. This paper presents LEASH-8, an eight-domain control model — identity, secrets, tool supply chain, approvals, containment, egress, observability, incident response — stated so that a small operation can implement it and, more importantly, evidence it: each domain carries a minimal implementation and an evidence test its owner must be able to satisfy in under a minute. Around the model are three instruments: a 24-statement scorecard with bands, a reference architecture in which the model plans, a deterministic gate authorizes and a scoped executor acts, and a checklist for designing the approval leg together with a catalogue of approval designs that fail it (including the one that fails by asking about everything and training its reader to stop looking). No novelty is claimed at the level of principles. Every domain restates least privilege, zero trust, capability security, the confused deputy, supply-chain integrity or operational monitoring; enterprise maturity models (OWASP, CSA) already cover this ground for organizations with security teams, CaMeL formalizes policy enforcement outside the model, and OpenPort specifies risk-gated review, time-bounded approvals and state revalidation. The paper includes a per-domain novelty ledger that says “no novelty” where that is the honest verdict. The contribution is operationalization for the operator who has no security team: the smallest defensible control set, the evidence question that makes each control checkable, and two open reference implementations. Patterns come from a five-machine production agent operation, and a grounding table marks every such claim as either backed by a public artifact or as unaudited operator experience. This is a design paper, not an evaluation: no user study, no benchmark of our own, and no measurement that a higher score produces fewer incidents — the paper states what would falsify it instead. Code: github.com/tonydzi/agent-leash (model, scorecard, checklist, reference A2A agent card, MIT) and github.com/tonydzi/agent-approval-gate (standard-library approval gate with decision classes and tests, MIT). title: A Resilient Microservices Architecture for AI-Powered Academic Assistant: Integrating Spring AI, RAG, and MCP Patterns
abstract: This record provides the draft and associated resources for the study entitled: "A Resilient Microservices Architecture for AI-Powered Academic Assistant: Integrating Spring AI, RAG, and MCP Patterns" This work presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of a distributed system for an AI-powered academic assistant, developed using a microservices architecture based on Spring Cloud. The system integrates Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Spring AI to enable domain-specific question answering grounded in structured data about academic faculty members. The architecture incorporates multiple modern software engineering and AI integration patterns, including:- Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for contextualized responses- Model Context Protocol (MCP) for structured interaction with internal and external data sources- Serverless processing using Spring Cloud Function- Resilience patterns (Circuit Breaker, Retry, Rate Limiter, Time Limiter) implemented via Resilience4j- Full observability using Prometheus, Grafana, and Zipkin The system was evaluated through load testing using Apache JMeter, demonstrating robustness under failure scenarios and the effectiveness of resilience mechanisms in preventing cascading failures. title: AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDOXX, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

title: Policy heterogeneity improves collective olfactory search in 3-D turbulence
abstract: We investigate the role of policy heterogeneity in enhancing the olfactory search capabilities of cooperative agent swarms operating in complex, real-world turbulent environments. Using odor fields from direct numerical simulations of the Navier-Stokes equations, we demonstrate that heterogeneous groups, with exploratory and exploitative agents, consistently outperform homogeneous swarms where the exploration-exploitation tradeoff is managed at the individual level. Our results reveal that policy diversity enables the group to reach the odor source more efficiently by mitigating the detrimental effects of spatial correlations in the signal. These findings provide new insights into collective search behavior in biological systems and offer promising strategies for the design of robust, bioinspired search algorithms in engineered systems.

title: MCPHunt: An Evaluation Framework for Cross-Boundary Data Propagation in Multi-Server MCP Agents
abstract: Multi-server MCP agents create an information-flow control (IFC) problem: faithful tool composition can turn individually benign read/write permissions into cross-boundary credential propagation -- a structural side effect of workflow topology, not necessarily malicious model behavior. We present MCPHunt, to our knowledge the first controlled benchmark that isolates non-adversarial, exact-match credential propagation across multi-server MCP trust boundaries, with three methodological contributions: (1) canary-based taint tracking that reduces propagation detection to objective string matching; (2) an environment-controlled coverage design with risky, benign, and hard-negative conditions that validates pipeline soundness and adds a matched alternative-value control (same tasks, distinct synthetic credentials); (3) completion-requires-secret (CRS) stratification that disentangles task-mandated propagation (faithful execution of verbatim-transfer instructions) from policy-violating propagation (credentials included despite the option to redact). Across 3,615 main-benchmark traces from 5 models spanning 147 tasks and 9 mechanism families, policy-violating propagation rates of 11.5-41.3% persist across all models. This propagation is pathway-specific (rates from 0.0% to 74.4% across mechanisms for GPT-5.4) and concentrated in browser-mediated data flows; under the matched alternative-value control, propagation persists (25.9% vs. 20.4%; the matched-pair CI spans zero, so the comparison neither distinguishes nor equates the two rates). A prompt-mitigation study across 3 models shows policy-violating propagation rates as low as 0.3% (98% relative reduction from baseline) while preserving 80.5% utility, but effectiveness varies across models, motivating data-flow-aware defenses beyond prompting. Code, traces, and the labeling pipeline are publicly available under MIT and CC BY 4.0.

title: AI Governance & Security Framework Landscape: Comparative Analysis of Substrate Governance, Runtime Security, and Legacy Frameworks in 2026 Agentic Systems
abstract: This reference document provides a comparative analysis of eight AI governance and security frameworks across six dimensions: layer of control, core model, what the framework secures, strengths, and gaps in 2026 agentic system environments. The analysis covers APR-Series substrate governance, A2AS runtime security, OWASP AI Security & Privacy Guide, OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, ISO/IEC 5338, NIST AI RMF, MITRE ATLAS, and MOSAIC. The central finding is that existing frameworks were designed for a world where AI systems were models wrapped in applications, prompt injection was the dominant failure mode, and actions were reversible. That world ended in 2025. The 2026 agentic environment requires governance at the substrate layer — the execution environment, authority envelope, and semantic boundaries that agents operate within — not merely at the application or runtime layer. APR-Series defines the substrate-level invariants that agentic systems must satisfy. A2AS provides the runtime enforcement mechanisms that operate within those invariants. All other frameworks in this analysis operate below the substrate layer or govern organizational processes rather than agentic system behavior. The gap between what we deploy and what we govern is where the real risk in 2026 agentic systems lives. This reference is designed to make that gap visible.

title: Policy Governed Agentic Commerce
abstract: AI agents are transitioning from informational assistants to ac- tive economic actors. While recent transactional protocols (e.g., x402, Agent Payments Protocol (AP2), Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP), Machine Payments Protocol (MPP)) standardize checkout and on-chain settlement, they neglect the judgment layer: verify- ing whether an agent should purchase a specific resource given its principal’s constraints. Today, this judgment relies on inference- time prompts, which suffer from stochastic compliance, attention dilution, prompt injection, and lack of audit trails. This paper introduces the Policy-Governed Agentic Commerce Engine (Sella), a dual-target architecture separating the Policy De- cision Point (PDP) from localized Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs). We implement a multi-modal evaluation framework across 10 eval- uation categories (for datasets, APIs, and composed workflows) to compile cryptographic Agent Data Cards. To prevent transaction- time failures, we design a PEP with budget reservation semantics that solves concurrent Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) budget escapes and dynamic price spoofing. We evaluate our engine (Sella) against prompt-engineered baselines using a benchmark suite (SellaBench) containing 104 listings. Experimental results show that our architecture reduces the hard constraint-violation rate to exactly zero, cuts token overhead by up to 99.3% (99.6% for input tokens), and maintains task utility under adversarial injection.

title: Infrastructure-Aware Runtime Protection of Co-Deployed AI Services at the Industrial Edge
abstract: In modern production lines, a single edge device simultaneously runs multiple AI services like a torque-control model, a vision inspector, a predictive maintenance routine. All these services run on the same CPU and same shared network segment. When the shared network segment saturates, the services do not crash. The services just produce outputs that are inaccurate or stale, and no longer reflect the plant's conditions. Our paper targets this class of silent, partial failure scenarios in Industrial Edge Systems. We treat each co-deployed service as an autonomous agent. We introduce the Runtime Criticality Score (RCS), which each service agent uses to express at any moment, its intrinsic utility and survival urgency under resource constraints. The score is computed from six normalized dimensions covering physical consequence, inference quality, input freshness, recent availability stress, actuator coupling, and available protective actions on the host. Its dimension weights are adjusted online through a lightweight Bayesian update driven by the type of disturbance currently observed, so the same service is ranked differently under a network delay than under thermal throttling. Agents publish their RCS to peers over an open, peer-to-peer discovery channel, and use it to negotiate three things without a central controller: (i) local threshold enforcement on their own host, (ii) migration to a willing peer when the current host can no longer protect them, (iii) reassignment of the coordination role when the incumbent coordinator is itself impaired. Beyond the immediate benefit of catching silent degradation, the framework contributes a concrete instance of decentralized, physically grounded agent coordination. Agents belonging to different owners can advertise capabilities, bid for protection, and reorganize across an open network.

title: The Dual State: Artificial Intelligence, Authoritarian Control, and the Crisis of Youth in Bangladesh (2014-2024)
abstract: This thesis examines the transformative and tumultuous decade in Bangladesh from 2014 to 2024, a period defined by the consolidation of power under Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and the Awami League, and a parallel socio-technological revolution. It argues that the Bangladeshi state has evolved into a "Dual State": one that projects an image of a "Digital Bangladesh" driven by economic growth and technological adoption, while simultaneously operating as an increasingly authoritarian regime that leverages these very technologies for surveillance, control, and the suppression of dissent. The paper analyzes this duality through three interconnected lenses: the strategic deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital tools for state security and public narrative control; the systematic quashing of student-led political movements and protests; and the resultant societal decay manifesting in a public health crisis, rising suicide rates, and criminality. Central to this analysis is the phenomenon of the "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector," a purported technological tool that symbolizes the regime's attempt to weaponize AI for political purposes. The thesis concludes that this decade has created a profound crisis among Bangladesh's youth, caught between the state's promise of a digital future and the grim reality of political suffocation and social despair. Keywords: digital authoritarianism, Sheikh Hasina AI Detector, Bangladesh student protests, Digital Security Act (DSA) 2018, mental health crisis Bangladesh, competitive authoritarianism, political repression, youth despair, bot networks astroturfing, Dual State BangladeshChapter 1: Introduction – The "Digital Bangladesh" Paradox The period from 2014 to 2024 stands as a definitive era in the history of Bangladesh. Marked by the unprecedented political dominance of Sheikh Hasina and the Awami League, this decade witnessed the realization of the party's flagship vision: "Digital Bangladesh." Initiated in 2009, this vision promised to leverage information and communication technologies (ICT) to propel the nation into a developed, knowledge-based economy. By the mid-2010s, the fruits of this policy were increasingly visible: widespread mobile internet penetration, a burgeoning IT sector, digitization of government services, and a growing sense of national pride in technological advancement. However, beneath this veneer of progress, a more sinister reality was taking shape. The general elections of 2014, boycotted by the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and its ally Jamaat-e-Islami, were marred by widespread violence and critically low voter turnout, granting the Awami League a virtually uncontested parliamentary supermajority. This electoral victory, while legally securing a term, fundamentally eroded the legitimacy of the democratic process and set the stage for an era of de facto one-party rule. The 2018 elections further cemented this trend, being widely criticized by international observers as deeply flawed. This thesis posits that these two narratives—the triumphant march of "Digital Bangladesh" and the descent into authoritarian governance—are not parallel stories but are intrinsically intertwined. The very technologies heralded as instruments of liberation and development were systematically co-opted as tools of control, surveillance, and narrative manipulation. This created a "Dual State": a Janus-faced entity where one face smiles upon foreign investors and the digital-savvy middle class, while the other grimaces with repression, silencing critics and crushing opposition. The primary victims and the most potent challengers to this Dual State have been the students and youth of Bangladesh. This demographic, the largest beneficiary of the digital revolution, has also been its most prominent casualty. This paper will explore the intricate connections between state policy, technological adoption, political repression, and the resulting socio-psychological crisis. It will investigate the following central research question: How has the Sheikh Hasina government's simultaneous pursuit of technological modernization and political authoritarianism between 2014 and 2024 contributed to a cycle of student protest, public health decline, and social crime? To answer this, the thesis is structured as follows: Chapter 2 outlines the political landscape, detailing the consolidation of the Awami League's power. Chapter 3 delves into the role of AI and digital technology, with a specific case study on the "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector." Chapter 4 analyzes the key student protest movements of the decade and the state's response. Chapter 5 examines the societal fallout, focusing on mental health, suicide, and crime. Finally, Chapter 6 synthesizes these threads to present a holistic conclusion on the state of the nation. Chapter 2: The Political Landscape – The Architecture of Authoritarian Rule (2014-2024) The period from 2014 onwards represents the solidification of a competitive authoritarian regime in Bangladesh. Under competitive authoritarianism, democratic institutions formally exist but are so heavily skewed in favor of the incumbent that they fail to meet minimum democratic standards. 2.1 The 2014 and 2018 Elections: A Democratic Façade The January 2014 general election was a watershed moment. The opposition BNP, demanding a neutral caretaker government to oversee the polls—a system abolished by the Awami League in 2011—resorted to a strategy of strikes, blockades, and boycott. The result was an election where over half of the parliamentary seats were uncontested, handing the Awami League a landslide victory. The pre-election period was marked by extreme violence, including arson attacks on public transport, for which both sides blamed each other. The election fundamentally broke the conventional pattern of power alternation in Bangladesh, establishing a "winner-takes-all" system where the stakes of losing power became existential for the opposition. The 2018 election continued this trend. While the BNP participated, its leader Khaleda Zia was imprisoned on charges widely seen as politically motivated, crippling the party's campaign. On election day, widespread allegations of ballot stuffing, voter intimidation, and falsification of results were reported. The Awami League and its allies won 288 of the 300 directly elected seats. The international community, while noting the irregularities, largely accepted the outcome, prioritizing strategic and economic interests over democratic principles. This tacit acceptance further emboldened the regime. 2.2 The Legal and Extralegal Apparatus of Control The government employed a multi-pronged strategy to neutralize opposition and dissent. The Digital Security Act (DSA) 2018: This legislation became the regime's most potent legal weapon. Its vague provisions, such as criminalizing speech that "hurts religious sentiment" or "spoils communal harmony," or spreads "propaganda and campaigns against liberation war spirit," were routinely used to arrest journalists, activists, academics, and ordinary citizens for critical social media posts. The non-bailable nature of the charges created a powerful chilling effect, stifling free speech in the digital public sphere that "Digital Bangladesh" had helped create. Enforced Disappearances and Extrajudicial Killings: Human rights organizations like Human Rights Watch and Odhikar have documented hundreds of cases of enforced disappearances by state security forces, predominantly targeting opposition members, activists, and dissidents. Many victims later reappeared in state custody, charged under laws like the DSA; others were found dead, with authorities claiming they were killed in "crossfires" or "gunfights"—a euphemism for extrajudicial killing that has entered the common lexicon. Co-option of Institutions: Key state institutions, including the judiciary, the election commission, and the anti-corruption commission, were widely perceived as having lost their independence and being used to harass the opposition and protect allies of the regime. This political context is the essential backdrop against which the technological and social developments of the decade must be understood. The state's insecurity and its drive for total control fueled its interest in advanced tools of surveillance and information management. Chapter 3: The AI Revolution – Tools for Development and Instruments of Repression The "Digital Bangladesh" vision was not merely rhetorical. The government made significant investments in digital infrastructure. Mobile internet users grew from a few million to over 120 million. Services like online tax filing, utility bill payments, and university admissions became digitized, improving efficiency and reducing low-level corruption. However, this digital transformation had a dark underbelly. The same infrastructure that delivered services also enabled unprecedented state surveillance. 3.1 The Emergence of Pro-Government AI and Bot Networks By the late 2010s, a sophisticated ecosystem of pro-government propaganda emerged online. While not all of it can be definitively labeled as "AI," it demonstrated a coordinated, automated, and strategic use of digital tools. Twitter/X and Facebook Bots: During periods of political tension or student protests, social media platforms would be flooded with accounts praising the government, Sheikh Hasina, and the Awami League, while simultaneously attacking and discrediting critics, protesters, and opposition figures. These accounts often used similar language, posted in coordinated bursts, and displayed other inauthentic behavioral patterns consistent with bot networks. Astroturfing and Narrative Control: These networks were used to create a false sense of popular consensus. When a controversial policy was introduced or a protest movement gained traction, these bots would swarm hashtags and comment sections, drowning out dissenting voices and projecting an image of overwhelming public support for the government. This tactic, known as astroturfing, is a form of information warfare that manipulates public perception. Deepfakes and Synthetic Media: While less prevalent, there were instances of manipulated media being used for political purposes. This included edited videos to make protesters appear violent or to spread disinformation about opposition leaders. The potential for more advanced AI-generated deepfakes to create chaos and discredit movements represents a significant future threat. 3.2 Case Study: The "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector" Phenomenon The most potent symbol of the regime's attempt to fuse technology with political control is the "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector." This is not a single, publicly available software application, but rather a purported technological capability that has been reported in state-aligned media and hinted at by government officials. The concept revolves around using Artificial Intelligence, specifically machine learning and Natural Language Processing (NLP), to monitor the Bangladeshi digital sphere (social media, news sites, blogs) in real-time. Its stated purpose, as per pro-government narratives, is to "detect anti-state propaganda," "fake news," and "defamatory content" against the Prime Minister, the state, and the ideology of the Liberation War. Technical and Ethical Analysis: Data and Training: For such a system to work, it would require a massive dataset of online content labeled as "loyal/pro-state" and "subversive/anti-state." The fundamental problem is the political nature of these labels. A critique of a government policy on electricity tariffs could be algorithmically classified as "anti-state" if the training data is curated by a partisan entity. This creates a feedback loop where the AI learns and reinforces the ruling party's political biases. Lack of Transparency: There is no public information about the system's algorithms, its false-positive rate, or its oversight mechanisms. This opacity makes it a perfect tool for arbitrary and politically motivated enforcement. A citizen could be flagged by a black-box algorithm for a seemingly innocuous post, leading to investigation or arrest under the DSA. Function as a Chilling Effect: The mere existence of such a tool, whether fully operational or partly a myth propagated to instill fear, serves a powerful psychological purpose. It creates a panopticon effect, where citizens self-censor, believing that an all-seeing AI is constantly monitoring their digital footprints. This directly undermines the freedom of expression that a healthy digital public sphere requires. The "Sheikh Hasina AI Detector" is thus the ultimate embodiment of the Dual State. It is a technologically advanced system, born from the "Digital Bangladesh" initiative, but its primary function is authoritarian: to identify, track, and neutralize political dissent. It represents the weaponization of AI not for national security against external threats, but for regime security against its own citizens. Chapter 4: The Fire of Protest – Student Movements and State Response The political repression and the weaponization of technology did not go unchallenged. The most significant and sustained challenges came from the student community, whose protests became flashpoints that revealed the true nature of the state. 4.1 The Quota Reform Movement (2018) In April 2018, university and college students across the country launched a massive movement demanding a reform of the quota system for government jobs. The existing system reserved 56% of posts for various groups (children of freedom fighters, women, districts, etc.), which protesters argued was unfair and promoted inefficiency. The movement was largely peaceful, organized by students themselves, and cut across partisan lines. The state's response was brutal. Police and ruling party student wing, the Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), violently attacked protesting students on campuses and on the streets. Dozens were injured, and hundreds were arrested. The government initially agreed to abolish the quotas but later backtracked after the movement was suppressed. The key takeaway was the state's intolerance of any large-scale, non-partisan mobilization that challenged a state policy, even one led by apolitical students. 4.2 The Road Safety Protests (2018) In July 2018, the death of two students by a speeding bus in Dhaka ignited long-simmering public anger over chaotic and unregulated transport systems. For days, thousands of school and college students occupied major intersections in the capital, enforcing traffic laws themselves in a stunning display of civic responsibility. The state's response was even more severe. The BCL, alongside police and armed plainclothes individuals, launched coordinated attacks on the protesters. There were numerous reports of sexual harassment of female protesters, beatings, and kidnappings. The digital tools of the state were also deployed: false narratives portraying the students as "hooligans" and "agents of conspirators" were spread online by bot networks. The "AI Detector" logic was implicitly at play, framing legitimate civic protest as an "anti-state" activity requiring a digital and physical crackdown. 4.3 The 2024 University Dues Hike Protests A more recent example in early 2024 saw protests at public universities like the University of Dhaka against sudden and sharp hikes in tuition and other fees. Students argued this would make higher education inaccessible for the poor and middle class. Once again, the state's response was to deploy police and the BCL to violently disperse gatherings, arrest protest leaders, and shutter dormitories. Pattern of Response: A clear pattern emerges from these protests: A legitimate, grassroots grievance sparks a student-led movement. The state perceives it not as a civic issue but as a challenge to its authority. It responds with a tripartite strategy: (a) physical violence through state and party actors; (b) a disinformation campaign online to discredit the protesters; and (c) legal persecution using laws like the DSA. This cycle of protest and violent suppression has had profound psychological consequences for a generation of young Bangladeshis. title: [Progress and perspectives of surface layer proteins from Bacillus species--a review].
abstract: S-layer proteins are crystalline arrays composed of numerous identical protein or glycoprotein subunits. They comprise the outermost cell envelope component in most archaea and many bacteria. The remarkable properties of S-layer proteins are their capability to self-assemble and specific binding, which give S-layer proteins a wide application potential in nanotechnology and biomimetics. Recently most study in this field was concerned on the S-layer proteins of Bacillus species. This review provided a brief survey of the current state of the study about the genetics, function, properties, pathogenic correlation and application of the S-layer proteins of Bacillus species. The aim of this review was to gain more knowledge about the function of S-layers and lead to the development of new types of surface display system and recombinant vaccines, diagnostic agents and biocompatible surfaces.

title: Alteration of DNA base excision repair enzymes hMYH and hOGG1 in hydrogen peroxide resistant transformed human breast cells.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Oxidative stress is a major causative agent of carcinogenesis, aging, and a number of diseases. 8-oxoG is the most stable and deleterious lesion of oxidative DNA damage. The 8-oxoG lesions can be eliminated by human repair systems consisting of three enzymes hMTH1, hOGG1, and hMYH homologous to E. coli MutT, MutM, and MutY proteins, respectively. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Human cells (P1, P2, and P3) resistant to H(2)O(2) were derived from the non-tumorigenic human breast cell line MCF10A by sequential treatment of the cells with H(2)O(2). The protein expression levels of DNA repair enzymes were analyzed by Western blotting. The DNA binding and glycosylase activities of hMYH and hOGG1 were measured in the extracts of the H(2)O(2) resistant cells. RESULTS: The H(2)O(2) resistant cells displayed tremendously greater anchorage-independent growth capability and higher expression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2 than the parental cells. H(2)O(2) detoxification ability was elevated in P1 and P2 cells, but not in P3 cells, suggesting P3 cells might employ a different defense mechanism from P1 and P2 cells. In P3 cells, both hOGG1 and hMYH glycosylase activities were reduced but their protein levels increased. Two A/8-oxoG binding complexes were detected with cell extracts: the fast-migrating complex (bottom form) was dominated in MCF10A cells, and was greatly reduced in P3 cells. Interesting, the P3 cells showing the least amount of bottom form had the weakest hMYH glycosylase activity. CONCLUSIONS: Our results demonstrated, for the first time, that alteration of base excision repair pathways is correlated to cell resistance to oxidative stress.

title: MCP Pitfall Lab: Exposing Developer Pitfalls in MCP Tool Server Security under Multi-Vector Attacks
abstract: Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables tool-integrated LLM agents, but its third-party tool-server ecosystem expands software supply-chain risk across tool metadata, untrusted outputs, cross-tool flows, multi-modal inputs, and privileged sink actions. Existing MCP benchmarks mainly measure robustness to malicious inputs, offering limited support for dependency vetting, semantic metadata auditing, and hardening regression. We present MCP Pitfall Lab, a protocol-aware security testing framework that models developer pitfalls as reproducible scenarios and validates outcomes using MCP traces and objective validators rather than agent self-report. We also introduce Semantic MCP-Bill-of-Material(MCP-BOM), representing that augments component inventory with security-relevant tool semantics, including descriptions, schemas, high-risk parameters, source/sink roles, trust boundaries, policy hooks, audit support, and trace provenance. Across 2,579 validator-completed runs over four models, Pitfall Lab observes 31.9% overall attack success rate(ASR), with multi-modal injection strongest at 38.7%. Semantic static fields detect pitfalls involving policy-bearing tool descriptions, permissive schemas, missing audit support, and absent server-side validation with F1=0.727, while BOM-backed findings drop from 27 to 16 after hardening. Decomposed risk metrics show Control Coverage increasing from 0.173 to 0.697 and Residual Risk decreasing from 15.31 to 6.09. A trace-linked case study further demonstrates that cross-tool forwarding and image-to-tool leakage require runtime provenance rather than static manifest fields alone. Overall, Pitfall Lab reframes MCP tool servers as AI software-supply-chain dependencies and provides BOM-backed artifacts for review, hardening, and trace-grounded regression testing

title: Soundtrack to a Movement: African American Islam, Jazz, and Black Internationalism
abstract: In Soundtrack to a Movement: African American Islam, Jazz, and Black Inter-nationalism, Richard Brent Turner composes an ambitious and interdisciplinary study that situates jazz music in Islamic religiosity at the heart of twentieth-century Black internationalism, bridging the worlds of religious studies, musicology, and Black diaspora to articulate a previously under-examined nexus: the intertwinement of African American Islam, jazz music, and Black international political imaginaries in the mid-twentieth century. Drawing from a diverse archive of musicians’ biographies, religious movements, Cold War cultural diplomacy, and performance histories, Turner argues that from the 1940s to the 1970s African American jazz musicians functioned as both spiritual seekers and internationalist actors. Through their artistic and religious commitments, these figures helped construct what Turner identifies as an emergent diasporic consciousness, what he terms a “Black Atlantic cool,” which operates as a performance of self-determination, transnational identification, and resistance to racial and imperial domination.The monograph centers iconic and under-recognized figures like John Coltrane, Yusef Lateef, Max Roach, Ahmed Abdul-Malik, Etta James, and Malcolm X, whose simultaneous engagement with jazz and Islam provided alternative modes of Black religiosity and cultural nationalism in the mid-twentieth century. Significantly, Turner resists a singular reading of Islam’s influence by attending to a plurality of Islamic currents, including the Ahmadiyya Muslim community, the Nation of Islam, and Sunni traditions. In doing so, he reconfigures Islam, not merely as a faith adopted by incarcerated converts or political radicals but as a dynamic transnational religion mediated through sound, movement, and improvisational theology.Soundtrack to a Movement is organized into four substantive chapters, framed by an introduction and a conclusion that collectively trace the historical relationship between African American Islam, jazz, and Black internationalism from the 1940s through the 1970s. Turner’s central argument is that jazz musicians were not merely artistic innovators but also religious and political actors whose conversions to Islam, and whose musical expressions of faith, function as a critical component of Black diasporic consciousness and anti-colonial solidarity.In the introduction, Turner establishes the interpretive scaffolding for the book’s central themes: Islam and jazz as parallel and interwoven modes of resistance, performance, and self-fashioning. He positions key figures like Malcolm X and John Coltrane as emblematic of this fusion, arguing that their spiritual and political trajectories reflected a broader turn among African American artists toward Islamic faith and global Black liberation. The introduction lays out the concept of “Black Atlantic cool,” a term Turner uses to describe a performative aesthetic and spiritual disposition cultivated by Black jazz musicians that bridged the sacred and the expressive, the individual and the transnational. This framework draws from and extends Paul Gilroy’s The Black Atlantic, situating jazz and Islam within a mutually constitutive diasporic geography.In chapter 1, “Islamic and Christian Influences in Jazz: Boston and New York during World War II,” Turner explores how jazz scenes in northern urban centers like Boston and New York became crucibles for religious experimentation. Turner centers Malcolm Little’s early exposure to bebop, Garveyism, and Islam through interactions with the Ahmadiyya Muslim community and Afro Caribbean immigrants. These Black Atlantic encounters helped lay the foundation for the convergence of Black religious internationalism and jazz performance. The chapter emphasizes the importance of local diasporic networks, particularly those shaped by the great migration and Caribbean migration, and facilitating new articulations of masculinity, spirituality, and musical identity.Chapter 2, “Turn to Allah, Pray to the East: Bebop and the Nation of Islam’s Mission to Black people in Prison,” focuses on the Nation of Islam’s (NOI) influence on imprisoned African American men and its ideological resonance with bebop’s avant-garde rebellion. Turner examines how the NOI’s theological formulations, rooted in racial separatism, Black self-reliance, and divine justice, intersected with the improvisational ethos of bebop to shape a distinctive performance of postwar Black masculinity. The chapter also situates Malcolm X’s prison conversion within this context and highlights the significance of music in both disseminating and embodying NOI ideology. This chapter resonates with Alex Lubin’s Geographies of Liberation, which treats Islam as an alternative transnational imagery, capable of linking U.S. Black communities to global anti-colonial movements across the Middle East and Africa.Chapter 3, “The Faith of Universal Brotherhood,” traces the influence of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community among bebop musicians in Boston, Detroit, and Chicago. Turner argues that the Ahmadi’s explicitly internationalist and anti-racist message resonated deeply with African American artists seeking spiritual and political alternatives to both white Christianity and domestic racial liberalism. Through case studies of musicians such as Yusef Lateef, Ahmed Abdul-Malik, and Talia Dawud, the chapter reveals how conversion to Ahmadiyya Islam facilitated access to transnational networks, particularly across the Indian subcontinent and West Africa, and provided a theological basis for musical innovation.Chapter 4, “Hard Bop, Free Jazz, and Islam,” brings the narrative into the 1960s, exploring how African American jazz musicians synthesized Islamic spirituality, Black Power aesthetics, and global Third World liberation discourses. Turner details how artists such as Coltrane, Max Roach, and Etta James embodied the confluence of musical experimentation and Islamic religiosity. This chapter also examines U.S. State Department jazz tours to Muslim-majority countries and Africa, reframing these diplomatic programs as ambivalent tools of Cold War cultural hegemony that were nevertheless repurposed by Black artists to articulate diasporic solidarity and anti-imperial critique.In the conclusion, Turner extends the genealogy of African American Islam and jazz into the post-Coltrane era, linking it to the emergence of Islam in hip-hop and the enduring appeal of Afro-diasporic spiritual internationalism. Figures such as Pharaoh Sanders and Alice Coltrane are portrayed as spiritual torchbearers of this legacy, blending musical transcendence with religious experimentation. Collectively, the book offers a compelling historical account of the mutually constitutive relationship between religion and sound in the Black radical tradition. Attention to urban geographies, spiritual pluralism, and diasporic connectivity significantly broaden prevailing understandings of Black internationalism.Richard Brent Turner’s Soundtrack to a Movement offers a necessary intervention into African American religious and cultural history by placing jazz musicians at the center of Black internationalist thought and spiritual experimentation. One of the book’s greatest strengths lies in its methodological synthesis: Turner draws on archival material, oral histories, music, criticism, and religious studies to construct a narrative that is at once richly historical and theoretically ambitious. By refusing to reduce African American Islam to a monolithic tradition, Turner highlights a pluralistic religious landscape that includes the Nation of Islam, the Ahmadiyya movement, and Sunni orthodoxy, each of which offered divergent theological frameworks and transnational affiliations. This is an important corrective to prevailing scholarship that often isolates Black Islam within prison conversion narratives or national politics.Turner’s most significant historiographical contribution is his insistence that Black music and Black religion were not separate spheres but mutually constitutive modes of diasporic world making. He treats jazz not merely as a sonic artifact but as a spiritual discourse and political language that enabled African American musicians to forge connections across borders and challenge hegemonic norms of citizenship, masculinity, and religiosity. The notion of “Black Atlantic cool,” borrowed from Robert Farris Thompson and recast in Turner’s own trans-religious idiom, functions as an organizing aesthetic and political concept, one that bridges sonic innovation with bodily compartment, Islamic piety, and diasporic masculinity.The book’s case studies are particularly compelling. For instance, Turner’s discussion of Yusef Lateef’s conversion to Ahmadiyya Islam and his incorporation of Arab and Asian instrumentation into his jazz composition reveals how religiosity often entailed musical hybridity. Lateef, for example, who was drawn to the ethical and rational appeal of Islam, explained: When Almighty God turns a person’s heart toward Islam (peace) there is no other choice for the person” (8). As Turner notes, Lateef “learned to play instruments from all over the world” (118), and his album Jazz for the Thinker expressed “his growing sense of the irrelevance of national boundaries when it came to both music and religion” (119). This deeply embodied transnationalism renders Lateef a paradigmatic figure in Turner’s narrative of Black religious internationalism.Similarly, John Coltrane’s spiritual evolution is mapped onto his musical trajectory, culminating in A Love Supreme as a sonic articulation of Black spiritual seeking, diasporic yearning, and political transcendence. Turner emphasizes Coltrane’s religious resonance with Islam by citing the phrase “Allah Supreme” embedded in the album’s performative structure, stating that “Coltrane makes the connection from A Love Supreme to Allah Supreme for his entire listening audience, forever delivering a sound of Islam to the world of American music” (191). Coltrane’s liner notes further signal of theological gravitation: “It is with God. He is gracious and merciful. His way is in love . . . A Love Supreme” (190). These analyses successfully resist biographical romanticization and instead locate artists within concrete urban, theological, and geopolitical contexts.Turner also intervenes in Cold War historiography through his analysis of the U.S. State Department jazz tours, building on earlier work by Penny Von Eschen in Satchmo Blows Up the World, which first established the jazz ambassador program as a site of both cultural diplomacy and subversion. Like Von Eschen, Turner acknowledges these programs as ambivalent sites of state power and Black resistance and complicates the celebratory narrative of jazz diplomacy. He acknowledges that jazz was “used by the US government to represent the values of freedom and democracy to audiences in Asia, Africa, and the Middle East” (130) but emphasizes how musicians like Dizzy Gillespie actively contested these narratives. As Gillespie famously remarked: “I wasn’t going over to apologize for the racist policies of America” (133). Turner thus highlights how African American performers converted government-sanctioned tours into moments of diasporic and anti-colonial solidarity.That said, the book is not without its limitations. One notable absence is a sustained treatment of gender and sexuality. While Turner does include brief reflections on Etta James and Alice Coltrane, the broader narrative remains heavily centered on male musicians and masculinist formulations of religious authority, resistance, and performance. Turner argues that Etta James, who briefly adopted the name, Jamesetta X, later cut her ties with Islam, a moment that does not fully explore the precarious positioning of Black women in these spiritual communities. He also acknowledges that “Islamic men in the jazz world sometimes shaped women’s constructions of Muslim-ness in both private and public relationships, in both positive and . . . negative ways” (117). Similarly, Alice Coltrane’s cosmology, blending Islamic, Hindu, and Black Christian mystical forms, is referenced only in passing, despite her centrality to post-Coltrane spiritual jazz. A more sustained engagement with Black women’s religious aesthetics, both within and beyond jazz, would have enriched the book’s claims about religious pluralism and diasporic spirituality. This presents a missed opportunity to engage with works like Cheryl Higashida’s Black Internationalist Feminism or Carole Boyce Davies’s Left of Karl Marx, both of which highlight the intellectual, artistic, and political labor of Black women in shaping diasporic and anti-imperial thought.Moreover, while Turner makes important gestures toward urban history, particularly in Boston, New York, and Philadelphia, his analysis sometimes privileges metropolitan centers to the exclusion of other diasporic centers. The inclusion of musicians’ experiences in Paris or Dakar, for example, is suggestive but underdeveloped. Given the book’s claim to narrate a “Black Atlantic” spiritual and musical tradition, a broader geographic scope beyond the U.S. East Coast might have sharpened the analysis. This is less of a flaw than an indication of the book’s generative possibilities for future scholarship.Theoretically, Turner is indebted to Paul Gilroy’s The Black Atlantic, but he also moves beyond Gilroy by emphasizing religion as a constitutive force in diasporic modernity. Where Gilroy privileges secular aesthetics, particularly music, as a form of transnational communication, Turner reintroduces the sacred as both epistemology and infrastructure. His insistence that jazz performance and Islamic belief were not discrete practices but rather entangled modes of Black self-fashioning reconfigures our understanding of the Black internationalist archive. In this sense, Soundtrack to a Movement resonates with recent scholarship by Sylvester Johnson, Edward Curtis, and Zareena Grewal, who have traced the global itineraries of African American Islam and its entanglements with empire, race, and modernity.Crucially, Turner avoids the teleological impulse to treat Islam as a resolution to the spiritual and political longings of African American musicians. Instead, he centers the iterative, experimental, and often contradictory nature of religious affiliation. Figures such as Malcolm X, Ahmed Abdul-Malik, and Rashied Ali are portrayed not as converts in a narrative of arrival but as travelers in a landscape of shifting affiliations, theological questioning, and sonic innovation. This emphasis on process over closure is one of the book’s methodological achievements.Finally, the book’s prose is both accessible and theoretically dense, striking a balance between historical narration and critical analysis. Turner writes with evident care for his subjects, neither romanticizing nor flattening their spiritual and political commitments. His archival breath and narrative clarity makes Soundtrack to a Movement suitable for advanced undergraduate and graduate classrooms, as well as for scholars and African American studies, religious studies, ethnomusicology, and diaspora studies.Soundtrack to a Movement makes a significant contribution to the growing body of scholarship on African American Islam, Black internationalism, and the cultural politics of jazz. By emphasizing religion as a generative site of diasporic identification and artistic experimentation, Turner challenges the secular assumptions that often underwrite scholarship on Black musical modernity. His archival recovery of figures such as Yusef Lateef, Ahmed Abdul-Malik, and Etta James, alongside more canonical subjects like Coltrane and Malcolm X, demonstrates the complexity and heterogeneity of Black religious expression in the mid-twentieth century. Importantly, Turner reframes jazz musicians not only as cultural producers but also as theorists of global Black liberation, whose sonic and spiritual practices extended beyond the boundaries of the United States and toward a transnational political horizon.What distinguishes Soundtrack to a Movement within the broader canon of Black diaspora scholarship is its insistence that religion, specifically Islam, is not peripheral but central to post-WWII formations of Black internationalism. This sets Turner apart from Paul Gilroy’s The Black Atlantic, which privileges secular aesthetic forms as the primary vehicle for diasporic connection. While Gilroy outlines a transatlantic counterculture of modernity rooted in political critique and cultural hybridity, Turner introduces the sacred as a constitutive infrastructure of diasporic belonging. His notion of a “Black Atlantic cool” explicitly builds on Gilroy, but through the idiom of Islamic piety, sonic experimentation, and spiritual affiliation, Turner generates a distinct modality of diasporic identity construction.Turner’s work also intersects with Brenda Gayle Plummer’s In Search of Power, which centers African American diplomacy in the age of decolonization. While Plummer emphasizes state actors and ideological alignments, Turner focuses on sonic and spiritual actors whose improvisational engagements with Islam allowed them to navigate and resist the logic of empire. Like Alex Lubin in Geographies of Liberation, Turner treats the Islamic Ummah as an alternative map of affiliation, an overlapping diaspora that complicates both national and Pan-African frameworks. Where CLR James emphasizes political revolt and Markist praxis, Turner shows how religion and music can also function as insurgent discourses of Black liberation. His intervention is perhaps closest to Hisham Aidi’s Rebel Music, though Turner’s archive is rooted in an earlier Cold War moment. Both authors emphasize Islam’s role in articulating global solidarities and rejecting racialized modernities, often through cultural performance and improvisation. In Turner’s narrative, the jazz musician is not merely a cultural agent but a diasporic theorist who speaks, resists, and dreams through both sound and belief.While the book would have benefited from a more sustained engagement with gender and a wider geographic purview beyond the U.S.-Africa axis, its conceptual clarity and historical depth render it a foundational text for future inquiries into the spiritual infrastructures of Black radicalism. For scholars of African American studies, religious studies, and Black diaspora studies, Turner’s work invites further interrogation into the affective, theological, and performative dimensions of Black internationalism.

title: Aspects of Social Responsibility in the Information Society
abstract: The Information Society must be based on fundamental assumptions about information and human information rights, access, privacy, self-determination and personal control rather than on privilege, power and special interest. Those involved in the planning, development and implementation of the information systems that turn the Information Society into a reality are the custodians of the greatest change agent yet devised. They must recognise their social responsibilities and act accordingly for the benefit of society and its citizens. This chapter serves as an illustration of what types of social responsibility issues need to be addressed, who must address them and how they might be addressed. It discusses some of the basic aspects of social responsibility and the implications for the Information Society, drawing in particular from Corporate Social Responsibility. Five disparate cases illustrate how concepts are turned into real organisational policy. Two example applications, electronic voting and electronic patient records are used to illustrate the types of social responsibility issues that need to be addressed in order to tackle the digital divide and satisfy the needs and aspirations of stakeholders.Request access from your librarian to read this chapter's full text.

title: Graph Agent Network: Empowering Nodes with Inference Capabilities for Adversarial Resilience
abstract: End-to-end training with global optimization have popularized graph neural networks (GNNs) for node classification, yet inadvertently introduced vulnerabilities to adversarial edge-perturbing attacks. Adversaries can exploit the inherent opened interfaces of GNNs' input and output, perturbing critical edges and thus manipulating the classification results. Current defenses, due to their persistent utilization of global-optimization-based end-to-end training schemes, inherently encapsulate the vulnerabilities of GNNs. This is specifically evidenced in their inability to defend against targeted secondary attacks. In this paper, we propose the Graph Agent Network (GAgN) to address the aforementioned vulnerabilities of GNNs. GAgN is a graph-structured agent network in which each node is designed as an 1-hop-view agent. Through the decentralized interactions between agents, they can learn to infer global perceptions to perform tasks including inferring embeddings, degrees and neighbor relationships for given nodes. This empowers nodes to filtering adversarial edges while carrying out classification tasks. Furthermore, agents' limited view prevents malicious messages from propagating globally in GAgN, thereby resisting global-optimization-based secondary attacks. We prove that single-hidden-layer multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) are theoretically sufficient to achieve these functionalities. Experimental results show that GAgN effectively implements all its intended capabilities and, compared to state-of-the-art defenses, achieves optimal classification accuracy on the perturbed datasets.

title: Automated Cyber Defense with Generalizable Graph-based Reinforcement Learning Agents
abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) is emerging as a viable strategy for automated cyber defense (ACD). The traditional RL approach represents networks as a list of computers in various states of safety or threat. Unfortunately, these models are forced to overfit to specific network topologies, rendering them ineffective when faced with even small environmental perturbations. In this work, we frame ACD as a two-player context-based partially observable Markov decision problem with observations represented as attributed graphs. This approach allows our agents to reason through the lens of relational inductive bias. Agents learn how to reason about hosts interacting with other system entities in a more general manner, and their actions are understood as edits to the graph representing the environment. By introducing this bias, we will show that our agents can better reason about the states of networks and zero-shot adapt to new ones. We show that this approach outperforms the state-of-the-art by a wide margin, and makes our agents capable of defending never-before-seen networks against a wide range of adversaries in a variety of complex, and multi-agent environments.

title: State Capacity in Seventeenth-Century France: The Role of the Intendants
abstract: Over the seventeenth century, France relied mainly on private agents to build its state capacity but it shifted gradually to public agents, the intendants. We document this centralization process. The intendants’ appointment occurred at different times across regions. Their alternating arrivals and departures in the regions created sequences of presence and vacancy that our empirical strategy takes advantage of. Using an original panel dataset, we identify a causal effect of the intendants’ presence on tax revenues, tax and food riots. Before the 1635 Edict that permanently installed them, occasional missions were operated by special envoys who turned to be effective immediately, but only in the provinces that kept the privilege to negotiate on taxation: there, tax revenues increased and tax riots decreased. Under Richelieu and Mazarin governments, from 1635 to 1660, these privilege-provinces resisted as the presence of the intendant triggered a decrease in tax revenues. In the less autonomous common provinces, tax revenues were collected but tax riots were caused by the intendant’s presence. Finally, the institution reached its maturity under the period that saw the arrival of Colbert from 1661 on: tax revenues increased sharply in both types of provinces but so did tax riots. The policies implemeted by Colbert and his successors helped bringing money in but could not prevent the population fromrebelling. Nor the regulations taken by the intendants were sufficient to cope with food riots.

title: A SwarmAI Testbed for Workforce Development and Collaborative, Interdisciplinary Research
abstract: Educating the next generation of AI researchers requires methods which teach the software tools, theoretical concepts, and domain knowledge specific to the field.To help develop these key skills, we focus particularly on the area of Swarm AI, which, in general, covers the autonomous operation of a large number of agents in a single environment.Applications of this field are numerous, including autonomous navigation, defense, robotics, logistics, and search/rescue.Despite the potential for impact in key problem domains and interdisciplinary nature, Swarm AI platforms are not generally used to develop competency in AI education.While some courses and tracks target AI in general, there are few tools to help engage learners in the specific area of Swarm AI.This is partly due to needing strong skills in the intersection of reinforcement learning, software development, and robotics, as well as a framework computing capability on which to test and evaluate.We propose Battle Optimized Laser Tag (BOLT), a Unity-built simulator that enables learners to develop Swarm AI algorithms in the context of a laser tag game between small mobile robots.The simulator is built to be familiar to a video game environment to maximize engagement, while the included documentation for the environment is designed as a gentle introduction into the topic of controlling swarms.Easily modified configurations enable educators to specify tasks and develop curricula to further challenge learners.Furthermore, the simulator is OS-agnostic, simple to install and uses Python to interface with the agents.This allows learners to implement their solutions on their own computers in a programming language common to other AI courses.Finally, extensions of the platform, leveraging the Python interface, can be deployed to physical robots or be used as a testbed for other AI domains beyond robotics including Human-Machine Teaming and Cybersecurity.

title: Art and ephemera post-structuralist perspective: visual art, ephemera and environment
abstract: A principal objective for this study was to investigate visual art that incorporates ephemera for conceptual and practical reasons. In my study, the ephemeron is not archived, it is intentionally allowed to disintegrate as an art process and I link this act through art praxis to potential metaphors for environmental wellbeing. My research identifies new approaches in art practice that address ecological strife. Poststructuralist theorising was applied to the visual arts to empower the ephemeral art object. The scope of this study involves potential locations or sites to effectively present and publicise this practice. Other than professional support from the art industry, the scope was broadened or restricted by an artist’s ability to respond with a very light environmental footprint to art and ephemera. Internet was a methodological strategy to counter what might have been isolation, and participants responded using email, from regions and centres. Thus it was significant for assembling data. My roles as artist, researcher and educator led to online communication and publication about this topic, and temporary art ~ installations I created for this study are a substantial part of this research. Mentors and models in the contemporary visual arts include professional creative arts practitioners and their work. Selected mentors (artists and authors) and models (current examples as well as precursors) assisted in identifying parameters for this study in a climate of global environmental change. Buskirk’s (2005) ‘contingent objects’ and Bourriaud’s (2002) ‘relational aesthetics’ are crucial for this study in recognising alternative approaches to ‘art history’. Selected theorists assisted methodological strategies to question the power of archived art as the art canon. Critical distinctions of ecological responsibility separate current art perspectives about land from some pre-1990 practice. Tiravanija’s the land (1998 - ongoing) includes key ideas that extend parameters for investigation of art not necessarily archived during or after installation, and he uses ecologically sensitive and informed approaches to comment on current environmental issues. Art collectives, such as the land, access the digital as a tool for ephemera and to counter regional isolation. Memory triggered by sight, and site as culture in nature, provided inspiration for this investigation, where art and nature are potentially interchangeable. Memory plays a role in identifying regeneration and transformation, evidenced in artist Wolfgang Laib’s materials: pollen, wax and milk; Gustav Metzger’s (1961) ‘acid nylon technique’ and his (2007) ‘shattered stones’ extend the scope of performative art objects, as does Sheela Gowda’s Collateral (2007), made from incense. Models from pre-1990 artwork and readymade precursors elucidate aesthetic of ephemera through time-based change. Post-structuralist theory and discourse analysis facilitated a revised positioning of visual art, through interaction of visual art and ephemera and how this impacts on contemporary society. My ‘Glossary for Art and Ephemera’ contributes to new knowledge. Through this theorizing glossary I invite dialogue from scholars, visual artists and the art industry. Neo-narrative and autobiographical voices query how the process of ephemera and disintegration could identify new visual arts practice, and how this practice impacts on decisions in disparate communities. Access and equity are discussed through facilitating artists’ stories into my study, as voices that have been excluded in the past. Agentic repositioning of art that privileges ephemera in a binary 2, as opposed to the archived, is predominant in this study. Analysis of the data empowers ephemera as art, and as metaphor to activate change in attitude to crisis in natural environment. Qualitative research assists the development of key questions about the relationship of visual artists’ concepts about material change and how they impact on the broader community’s environmental concern. Material investigation played an important part in the thesis, for though ‘art and ephemera’ is anti-archive, the disintegration and ephemeral nature of art materials are key to the art discussed in this thesis. This study presents a humble practice and materials ranging from pollen, fading photographs and incense to flotsam, detritus or garden mulch. The study identified art methods that empowered the ephemeron in visual art to act as a metaphor for the implementation of potential new policies for sustainable modes of practice in and beyond the visual arts. These apply to creative arts models for social and pedagogical application that could relieve stress caused by excess of commodity. These provide ways to address environmental concern. I have accumulated significant data and refer to this to provide recommendations for educational curriculum development to suggest that art and ephemera be considered as a viable and pragmatic alternative to, and not a replacement for, archival practice. Authors referenced for practice-based research and pedagogy, include Davies, Ashton, Foucault, Sullivan and Thompson. James Cook University research strength, People Identity Place, supports my regional influences from northwest Queensland. My original home, with naturally treeless plains, lies between the watershed for the Lake Eyre Basin and the Gulf of Carpentaria. Significant ideas emerged for my artwork from this region that is dry for most of any year. Sketches, diaries and archived photographic records contribute to my reflection on place. My findings inform researchers about the relationship of artists as cultural providers and communicators of ecologically sensitive issues. These methods demonstrate concern for the twenty-first century environmental situation identified by Stern (2007). Though much has been discussed and created in the area of art and social change, this research project identifies changes apparent in the natural environment, to act as creative visual art metaphors to increase awareness of climate change. ‘Art and ephemera’ is asserted as a viable alternative to archival art. Forms of art and ephemera exist as statements about conditions of change, and, of these, key pieces illuminate the impact of people in their own natural environmental location and how this could be addressed through change of attitude. My concern for regional place and environment led to development of my art praxis that comments on, and addresses, human activity and impact on place.

title: Refusal is Not Safety! Benchmarking Latent Safety Risks of LLM-Driven Content Humorization
abstract: Safety defenses for large language models (LLMs) have been extensively studied, with existing approaches focusing on attack detection and refusal mechanisms. Such fixed-form direct refusal strategies may introduce the risk of prefix injection attacks. Recent work has explored a new direction that leverages humor as an indirect refusal mechanism to mitigate over-refusal in jailbreak scenarios and reduce prefix injection risks. However, this approach implicitly assumes that humorous responses are safe. Whether humorization itself introduces safety risks remains unexplored. To address this issue, we conduct an exploratory study involving over 30,000 real-world agent interaction records and 45 stand-up comedians, revealing practical safety concerns in LLM-based content humorization. Motivated by these findings, we propose \textsc{HumorSafe}, a novel framework for evaluating latent safety risk propagation during humorization. \textsc{HumorSafe} enables LLMs to learn harmful humorization patterns and use them to transform benign content into humorous content with safety risks. Across five frontier LLMs, we find that LLMs can introduce stereotypes and toxicity during humorization. We further propose \textsc{HumorPIA}, a prompt injection attack that exploits latent risks in humor-based defenses. \textsc{HumorPIA} preserves the appearance of safe humorous refusal while covertly injecting harmful content, allowing latent risks to evade existing detection mechanisms. Experiments show that it increases toxicity by 3.14$\times$ while maintaining an apparent safety rate of 97.8\% even under defense settings. Our findings highlight a gap in existing LLM safety evaluations under humorized settings.

title: Federated Deep Reinforcement Learning for Energy Efficient Multi-Functional RIS-Assisted Low-Earth Orbit Networks
abstract: In this paper, a novel network architecture that deploys the multi-functional reconfigurable intelligent surface (MF-RIS) in low-Earth orbit (LEO) is proposed. Unlike traditional RIS with only signal reflection capability, the MF-RIS can reflect, refract, and amplify signals, as well as harvest energy from wireless signals. Given the high energy demands in shadow regions where solar energy is unavailable, MF-RIS is deployed in LEO to enhance signal coverage and improve energy efficiency (EE). To address this, we formulate a long-term EE optimization problem by determining the optimal parameters for MF-RIS configurations, including amplification and phase-shifts, energy harvesting ratios, and LEO transmit beamforming. To address the complex non-convex and non-linear problem, a federated learning enhanced multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (FEMAD) scheme is designed. Multi-agent DDPG of each agent can provide the optimal action policy from its interaction to environments, whereas federated learning enables the hidden information exchange among multi-agents. In numerical results, we can observe significant EE improvements compared to the other benchmarks, including centralized deep reinforcement learning as well as distributed multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG). Additionally, the proposed LEO-MF-RIS architecture has demonstrated its effectiveness, achieving the highest EE performance compared to the scenarios of fixed/no energy harvesting in MF-RIS, traditional reflection-only RIS, and deployment without RISs/MF-RISs.

title: Avatar-Bounded AI Evaluation A Contained Embodiment Framework for Single- and Multi-Agent Examination
abstract: Avatar-Bounded AI Evaluation proposes a containment-oriented framework for evaluating advanced AI systems without granting the underlying models unrestricted access to external tools, networks, filesystems, or execution environments. The central idea is to separate model intelligence from external agency. Each model is coupled to a constrained virtual embodiment, or avatar, whose sensory and action capabilities are explicitly bounded. All interactions with the evaluation environment are mediated through this avatar and an independent policy gate. The architecture therefore aims to preserve a fixed external action envelope even as the cognitive capability of the underlying model increases. The framework is first defined for single-agent evaluation and then extended to multi-agent examination arenas, where multiple AI systems can be placed inside the same closed environment. Communication between agents is restricted to observable channels, enabling controlled study of cooperation, collusion, rule violations, deceptive coordination, whistleblowing, supervision sensitivity, and emergent group behavior. Formally, the work introduces an avatar-mediated causal structure in which no direct model-to-environment action edge is permitted. The proposed design emphasizes complete mediation, bounded action spaces, controlled communication, and explicit separation between intelligence growth and externally available authority. The manuscript also outlines experimental protocols for testing whether advanced AI systems attempt unauthorized coordination, exploit evaluation rules, behave differently under observation, or cooperate with adversarial agents. This work is a theoretical research manuscript. It does not report deployed-agent experiments, human-subject studies, or empirical claims of demonstrated safety. Its contribution is the specification of a containment and evaluation architecture, formal properties of the proposed boundary, testable hypotheses, and a structured research program for single- and multi-agent AI evaluation. Keywords: AI safety; AI containment; multi-agent systems; AI evaluation; embodied AI; agentic AI; sandboxing; AI control; collusion; evaluation integrity; frontier AI; constrained agency.
